title: Bitcoin: Drawdown, Trading Activity and Market Risk
content:
Bitcoin's market size and its distance below its own price record answer different questions. The comparison above puts BTC beside other tracked assets from the same UTC market date. It separates drawdown from reported trading activity and shows how each feeds TokenRadar's score. The observations refresh with the dataset; this editorial explanation was revised on 2026-11-04.

| Research question | Evidence to inspect |
| :--- | :--- |
| Is BTC closer to its record than its peers? | BTC drawdown versus the peer median above |
| Is reported trading activity unusually high? | 24h volume divided by market cap, using the same date |
| Which inputs raise the score? | Four contributions, each capped at 2.5 points |
| Can the comparison be reproduced? | Download the observation and peer inventory JSON |

## Bitcoin's size does not remove drawdown risk

Bitcoin uses proof of work, with full nodes independently validating blocks against consensus rules. That describes a network security mechanism, not a guarantee about BTC's dollar price. The [Bitcoin developer guide](https://developer.bitcoin.org/devguide/block_chain.html) explains that distinction at the protocol level. A market risk comparison should therefore begin with observed prices and trading activity rather than assuming that a long operating history prevents a large loss.

Read BTC's percentage below its all-time high beside the peer median in the comparison. A smaller percentage means BTC is closer to its own record than the middle observation in this particular sample. It does not establish that BTC is cheap, expensive, or likely to recover. The reference price is a historical extreme, and an asset can remain below that extreme for a long period. Our [market risk distribution](/research#risk-distribution) adds the wider coverage context.

The sample excludes Bitcoin itself, gives each eligible peer equal weight, and requires matching UTC market dates. That prevents BTC's large capitalization from dominating the comparison. It also means the result describes a typical covered asset rather than the return or drawdown of an investable, capitalization-weighted portfolio. Stablecoins, small assets, and category overlap can affect the peer mix. Inspect the downloadable peer inventory before applying the result to a narrower investment universe.

## Trading activity is a liquidity clue, with limits

The turnover comparison divides reported 24-hour dollar volume by market capitalization. This makes activity comparable across assets of very different sizes. A large dollar volume can coexist with a modest turnover ratio when capitalization is especially large. Read the dollar volume in the market panel alongside the ratio rather than choosing only the more impressive-looking number.

Neither number measures the spread or available orders at a specific venue. A reader checking executable liquidity still needs the relevant trading pair's order book, expected slippage, venue access and fees. The [liquidity depth guide](/learn/liquidity-depth) explains that separate check. TokenRadar's table describes reported activity; it cannot establish that a particular order can be filled at the displayed reference price.

The score's volume input assigns 2.5 points at turnover of 1% or less and zero points at 10% or more, interpolating between those thresholds. Capitalization contributes zero points at $10 billion or more and reaches 2.5 points at $500 million or less. These are disclosed modeling choices, not universal boundaries between safe and unsafe markets. See the [methodology](/about#methodology) and the contribution table to understand their effect on BTC's total.

## Why the volatility date matters

The price-window dates appear above because the cached historical series can end before the market snapshot. A fresh spot price does not make an older volatility observation current. The calculation uses the coefficient of variation of the retained price levels, not annualized return volatility. Treat it as a description of that window and check its end date before interpreting the combined score.

Each risk input contributes at most 2.5 points. The four contributions are summed, rounded, then bounded between 1 and 10. Consequently, two assets can share a score while having quite different drawdown, size, turnover and volatility profiles. The contribution table is more informative than treating a one-point difference as a precise measurement of future losses. These inputs also leave custody failures, venue interruptions and protocol incidents outside the calculation.

## Supply rules and custody need separate verification

Bitcoin's issuance schedule approaches a maximum of 21 million BTC; the [Bitcoin FAQ](https://bitcoin.org/en/faq#how-are-bitcoins-created) describes issuance and its limits. This rule helps interpret the supply panel, but it does not determine demand or a dollar valuation. Distinguish BTC held directly from a custodial claim or a wrapped asset, where additional systems affect access and redemption.

For self-custody, confirm the receiving network, verify the destination and understand recovery before transferring funds. Our [Bitcoin storage guide](/bitcoin/transfer-to-ledger) covers the operational checklist. For venue research, review [how slippage affects execution](/learn/understanding-slippage). Neither the observed score nor a historical price record substitutes for those checks.

## FAQ

**What is unusual about Bitcoin in this comparison?**

The table identifies BTC's drawdown, turnover and score beside the same-date peer medians. The largest contribution difference highlights which measured input most separates it from the peer mean; the finding changes when the underlying dataset changes.

**Does a smaller drawdown predict a better return?**

No. Distance from a record describes the path already observed. It does not estimate a future target or assign a probability to a recovery.

**Where can I check the figures?**

Download the comparison JSON above for the asset, peer identities, input dates and unrounded contributions. Check the [CoinGecko Bitcoin record](https://www.coingecko.com/en/coins/bitcoin) for the upstream market source; a current source page may differ from this retained snapshot.

**What should I research next?**

Compare the observations with the [market risk distribution](/research#risk-distribution), then check which assets the broader index covers. Keep market updates separate from the editorial date when recording your own research.
